articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO live updates: AI lab tops $2 trillion market cap after record offering
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO live updates: AI lab tops $2 trillion market cap after record offering
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share in the artificial intelligence lab's Nasdaq debut on Thursday after the company completed the biggest initial public offering on record.
The stock will trade under the ticker "ANT" after the company raised $81.3 billion in the IPO. The Claude creator sold 980 million shares at $83 a piece on Wednesday, lifting the size and price of its offering.
The 5-year-old company captivated the corporate world with its Claude AI models and products, which have fueled its meteoric rise this year. Anthropic said in its prospectus that it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up a staggering 1,200% from the same period last year.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic has faced sharp criticism over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, including by President Donald Trump and other senior government officials.
CNBC's reporters are covering Anthropic's IPO live on air and online from our bureaus in San Francisco and Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, and from the Nasdaq in New York City.
Trading volume in Anthropic on its first day on the Nasdaq has already surpassed the number of SpaceX shares that were traded in its debut.
As of mid-day, more than 640 million Anthropic shares had changed hands. On SpaceX's opening day in June, a total of 522 million shares were traded.
Anthropic is also the most actively traded stock on the Nasdaq.
Anthropic has made headlines in recent months for its advanced artificial intelligence models with sophisticated cybersecurity capabilities.
In a bid to curb bad actors from exploiting them, the AI lab then limited access to select customers through Project Glasswing.
Anthropic has since broadened the pool of testers and launched a cybersecurity initiative aimed at protecting critical infrastructure. But these moves have raised questions over whether the company will scale its cybersecurity business — or even pit it against major security vendors, including partners.
Cybersecurity could match Anthropic's coding opportunity and reach $500 billion annually, Wolfe Research analysts wrote in a Thursday note.
"Act 2 is Cyber which given the last week seems like it could be as big as Coding," they wrote.
That market might include AI security operations, patching or penetration testing — simulated cyberattacks utilized to identity a company's security weaknesses.
"We think that model providers will offer a solution to replace the security team that is manually analyzing data with agents who can respond at machine speed," they added.
Wall Street banks are set to reap a huge windfall from Anthropic's IPO, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley among the biggest earners.
The company disclosed in its latest SEC filing that it agreed to pay the banks $550 million, surpassing the roughly $500 million payday banks took in from SpaceX's IPO in June.
Anthropic's investors and other partners are taking a victory lap upon the AI lab's successful debut.
Investors Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed dedicated the front page of their websites to congratulating Anthropic, as did counsel Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati . Bessemer's Byron Deeter posted a thread on X detailing the backstory of the firm's investment in Anthropic.
Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy, an early Anthropic investor, said the firm's aggregate position in the AI company is around $25 billion.
"Clearly the most epic return for Menlo Ventures in our history, and one of the top handful in the history of venture capital," Murphy told CNBC in an interview. "We feel grateful. We have over five LPs that we've delivered over a billion dollars of returns to, and at the end of the day, that's really our job."
Ashton Kutcher congratulated Dario Amodei and "the whole team at Anthropic" in a post on X shortly before the AI company's first trade.
Kutcher co-founded Sound Ventures , a Los Angeles-based venture capital firm, which invested in Anthropic in 2023 and participated in several subsequent funding rounds. The VC firm also counts Guy Oseary, the legendary talent manager for musicians including Madonna, among its cofounders.
Bloomberg reported that Sound Ventures owns roughly half a percent of Anthropic, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Sound Ventures' stake is likely now worth billions of dollars after the company's lofty IPO.
Byron Deeter, a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, called Anthropic 's IPO a " Google moment" for the frontier lab during CNBC's Halftime Report.
At over $2 trillion in market capitalization, Anthropic has entered Google's ranks as one of the most valuable companies in the world, behind Apple , Microsoft , Nvidia , Alphabet (Google's parent company), and Amazon .
But Deeter says Anthropic doesn't need to "dominate intelligence" in the same way that Google dominates search.
The artificial intelligence ecosystem will see "multiple great businesses," Deeter says, adding that he expects Anthropic to continue to be a market leader while also pacing the frontier of AI model development.
Anthropic has an unusual governance structure .
The company is a public benefit corporation, which means it's required to balance the financial interest of stockholders, the best interests of those affected by its conduct and its "company purpose." Anthropic said in its prospectus that its purpose is to facilitate the "responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."
Anthropic's seven co-founders also wield a lot of power over the company. Prior to the completion of its offering, Anthropic issued a single share of Class F common stock to a limited liability company called "Founder LLC." Anthropic's co-founders are the sole members of Founder LLC, and the entity holds 50.1% of the voting power of the company's outstanding shares.
Each co-founder sold 3.38 million shares in the IPO, according to the prospectus, for total proceeds of $1.96 billion.
Additionally, Anthropic introduced an independent governance body called the " Long-Term Benefit Trust " in 2023, which has the authority to elect and remove the majority of the company's board of directors.
Anthropic opened with a market capitalization of nearly $2.01 trillion, behind only Apple , Microsoft , Nvidia , Alphabet and Amazon .
Ben Bernanke, the former chair of the Federal Reserve , is in the room at the Nasdaq as investors celebrate Anthropic's first trade.
Anthropic in July appointed Bernanke to its Long-Term Benefit Trust, the AI company's independent governance structure that advises it and appoints its board members.
Anthropic shares popped 34% in the company's Nasdaq debut.
Anthropic is indicated to open at $111 per share, a person familiar told CNBC.
Anthropic is indicated to open at $110 a share, a person familiar told CNBC.
Amodei told JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon in a fireside chat on Friday that he thinks talent and culture are the "most important things" that drive a company's success, which is why he and his co-founders have tried to place so much emphasis on those areas at Anthropic.
Anthropic requires every employee to pass a culture interview, which is taken very seriously, Amodei said. He added that he spends roughly half of his time focusing on talent and culture at the company.
"We've been very disciplined about turning down people who are deeply technically talented, but who don't fit our culture," Amodei said. "We don't want people who are jerks. We don't want people who try to steal the show and don't work well with others. We don't want people who aren't oriented towards the public benefit."
Amodei also regularly holds DVQs, which stands for "Dario Vision Quests," where he speaks in front of the entire company. He said he tries to update employees by talking honestly and avoiding "corpo speak."

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.content_orig:
It was the first-ever meeting of the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers—one that host Xi Jinping opened by hailing its “pioneering significance.”
Exactly what was achieved when Xi met with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump at Kylin Villa in northwestern Shenzhen on Thursday, however, has onlookers scratching their heads. Xi started by invoking the responsibility of Great Powers toward world peace; Putin delved into historic “shared interests;” while Trump immediately lashed out at “rogue globalist organisations,” such as the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ICC “has gotten out of control,” Trump told his companions seated around a round wooden table, and has “really strayed far beyond its jurisdiction.”
It was almost as if this historic trilateral , held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, didn’t have any fixed agenda. It hadn’t. When the confab was first proposed, Putin wanted to talk about Ukraine, though U.S. officials pushed back. Trump instead suggested nuclear arms and Iran, but Beijing wasn’t keen. Finally, China’s Foreign Ministry settled on “safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations.”
It was therefore an occasion rich with platitudes but not a lot else. “In this global village, major countries shoulder special responsibilities,” said Xi, who also called for the destruction of all nuclear weapons. “Positive interaction among major powers is not an optional question, but a compulsory one.”
Still, the meeting served its purpose. Trump gained a chance to project influence after chastening midterms and the unfolding Nvidia saga that forced the resignation of his close friend Jensen Huang as CEO. Xi got to flaunt himself as the consummate statesman, while Putin took a baby step out from the diplomatic cold. But it was also a distinctly unsettling sight for the U.S. President to be sitting beside two of America’s most consequential adversaries, whose governments declared in 2022 that their friendship with each other had “no limits.”
Before the three-way meeting, Trump met separately with Putin and then Xi. His roughly 40 minutes with the Russian President began on a hopeful note: “Wonderful things can come out of this—or at least start,” Trump said. During an hour of talks with Xi, Trump returned to a more familiar concern. “I’ll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” he said. He also suggested that Washington and Beijing could work together to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
That prospect mattered to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said Wednesday that the war could end in a single meeting if the U.S. and China used their economic leverage against Moscow. Instead, Trump launched a broadside against the ICC, which has issued an arrest warrant against Putin for war crimes, urging his autocratic counterparts to cooperate on “ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty.”
Trump also said it was “vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world,” before segueing into a justification of his war in Iran : “That’s what we’re doing in Iran. We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Of course, this was always going to be an occasion that would put style over substance. On Wednesday, Xi surprised onlookers by greeting a clearly delighted Trump on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan Airport. Their handshake turned into a brief hug, before five People’s Liberation Army J-10C fighter jets flew overhead, billowing red, yellow, and blue smoke.
In personally meeting Trump as he deplaned Air Force One, Xi reciprocated the welcome he received from the U.S. President at Joint Base Andrews in September. The gesture was a first by a top Chinese leader since Mao Zedong met Nikita Khrushchev at Beijing’s airport in 1959.
Putin had to suffice with being greeted by Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi, upon his earlier arrival in the wee hours of Wednesday morning. But Xi spent much of that afternoon in talks with his embattled Russian counterpart, who used his speech to assembled CEOs to lambast Western sanctions, crowing that the U.S. and Europe had “punished themselves” with punitive measures, which Russia had successfully sidestepped anyway.
Upon emerging from his two-hour bilateral with Putin, Xi called on both countries to “lead and advance … the democratization of international relations.” Putin, in turn, boasted that economic coercion was “a thing of the past.” Later in the evening, Putin and Trump shook hands before the gala dinner as Xi looked on smiling.
“Beijing’s top priority would be to create a more stable external environment for China’s development, particularly by making relations with Washington more predictable while maintaining steady cooperation with Moscow,” says Sun Chenghao, a fellow with Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy.
Still, the summit threatened to be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal, with company founder Huang admitting an affair with a woman accused of illicitly funneling chips to China and whom U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly suspect may be a Chinese spy. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim rule aimed at stopping Chinese firms from accessing advanced U.S. chips through data centers abroad.
Trump told Fox News that he and Xi “spoke the whole evening” during Wednesday’s gala dinner but only “briefly” discussed Nvidia. Trump also claimed he was unaware of the espionage allegations, which China vehemently denies. “I haven’t heard that she was a spy,” Trump said. “She was a businesswoman who bought chips, and who knows if they were bought right or wrong.”
Trump also appeared to shoot down any hopes of regulation governing AI: “We oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle [AI], and we won’t allow that to happen,” he said.
Still, the historic trilateral did succeed in visibly placing China at the center of Great Power diplomacy. Hosting the leaders alongside APEC supports Beijing’s claim that global influence is shifting eastward, with China as a stabilizing power, particularly amid unpredictable U.S. policy.
“The optics might actually play well for China,” says Chong Ja Ian, a professor of international relations at the National University of Singapore. “It certainly would fit the sort of image that Beijing and Xi would like to create for themselves.”
But while APEC was created in 1989 to ease trade and investment across the region, today’s world has been gripped by rising protectionism. The Trump Administration has levied tariffs on 60 trading partners that together account for 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. Moreover, Europe is increasingly chary about cheap Chinese exports that Brussels says are fueled by subsidies and industrial overcapacity.
Xi used his Wednesday address to business leaders to promise a more open Chinese market and present the world’s second-largest economy as a source of opportunity. “History tells us that opening doors brings progress while closing doors leaves one behind,” he said.
Yet the image of three elderly leaders debating global problems behind closed doors sits uneasily beside Xi’s call for a more multipolar world. Pro-Kremlin media was especially keen to frame the meeting as Yalta 2.0 after the historic powwow between Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill toward the end of World War II.
But it is Ukraine’s plucky defiance of that invasion that underscores how today’s Middle Powers have more agency. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged third countries to work together on trade, security and technology in order to shape the rules and resist economic coercion. “Middle powers must act together because if you are not at the table, you are on the menu,” Carney said.

articles.title_orig: TSMC tightens China AI chip curbs as new US rules close manufacturing loophole, sources say
articles.title_zh: TSMC tightens China AI chip curbs as new US rules close manufacturing loophole, sources say
articles.content_orig:

Chinese technology firms are bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans as the U.S. tightens restrictions on China 's access to the world's cutting-edge chips.
Chinese tech giant Alibaba , which on Thursday announced another quarter of strong revenue growth for its global AI cloud and compute services, warned that the new U.S. rules could affect some of its global data center expansion plans. It said it was still assessing the repercussions.
The Trump administration this week issued new rules in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, following the news that he’d had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
The rules now restrict remote computing access through data centers in third countries, the latest U.S. move to curtail China’s abilities to use advanced Nvidia chips to train its increasingly capable AI models.
Alibaba's AI revenues are surging as demand grows
As the technology race between the two superpowers intensifies, existing U.S. export restrictions already barred China from getting the world’s most powerful chips.
But some Chinese companies have been able to bypass those restrictions by renting remote computing access to train AI models, pushing the U.S. to close what some policymakers called a loophole.
As global AI usage grows, Alibaba has been expanding its capabilities across chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. It launched its flagship Qwen4-Max AI model earlier this week. In September, Alibaba's CEO called its new Zhenwu V900 chip the “most powerful” AI chip in China, while it announced massive data center investment plans in China and abroad.
Alibaba Cloud’s AI-related revenue currently comes significantly from China and there’s still a lot of “untapped demand” from Chinese enterprises, said Jacob Cooke of the Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies.
For the latest July-September quarter, Alibaba reported a 53% year-on-year revenue surge for its AI cloud and compute services to nearly 61 billion yuan ($9 billion). Total revenue for the quarter rose 10% from the year before to almost 272 billion yuan ($41 billion), slightly better than what analysts had expected.
While the company has a strong cash buffer, capital expenditures jumped 60% during the quarter to 50.5 billion yuan ($7.6 billion) thanks to its increased spending on AI infrastructure buildout.
Tencent says US chip curb ‘sets everyone back in China’
Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday said the new U.S. rule on chip access “sets everyone back in China.”
“Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China,” Tencent President Martin Lau said on an earnings call. Training timelines for Tencent’s next versions of its AI models would probably be impacted, he said.
“Chinese AI firms are still heavily dependent on the most frontier Nvidia chips," said James Chai, a researcher at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, with new U.S. rules on remote access cutting off a huge portion of Chinese firms’ access to compute.
A study released in October by the Institute for Progress, a U.S. think tank, estimated that remote access to AI chips through overseas data centers could account for roughly one-third of China’s AI compute by the end of 2027.
Nvidia, meanwhile, said it is now “no longer shipping” chips including the H200, one of its more powerful chips, though not the most advanced, although the Trump administration greenlighted some sales to China, reflecting how Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following Huang’s ouster.
Analysts expect the U.S. will step up its chip export control policies against China after Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, raised U.S. national security concerns. Earlier reporting by The New York Times suggested that U.S. officials suspected Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited in part to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available to Chinese companies.
Beijing has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, and has called the new U.S. rules blocking Chinese companies' remote access to computing power overseas “economic coercion.”
Analysts and industry leaders in China say the U.S.’s tightening of chip export control measures would ultimately accelerate China’s push to make its domestic chip industry self-sufficient.
“Over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we actually see the industry is actually progressing very fast,” said Tencent's Lau.

articles.title_orig: Critics Say Trump Fell Asleep During Xi’s Speech in China
articles.title_zh: Critics Say Trump Fell Asleep During Xi’s Speech in China
articles.content_orig:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title_orig: White House pool have phones taken away on return from China as speculation mounts over unscheduled stop
articles.title_zh: White House pool have phones taken away on return from China as speculation mounts over unscheduled stop
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
White House reporters traveling aboard Air Force One had their phones temporarily confiscated before President Donald Trump’s plane took off after his trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, raising the specter of an unscheduled detour on his way back to Washington D.C.
U.S. officials collected reporters’ devices as the president’s plane prepared to leave Shenzhen, China, Thursday evening.
“At 6:45 pm consider this your wheels up,” the White House pool report read. “Our phones are being taken away for now for security reasons.”
No one on the trip has provided more information. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for more information.
It is highly unusual for reporters’ phones to be sequestered outside of situations when the president is traveling to a war zone, such as when Trump flew to Al Asad Air Base in Iraq at Christmas in 2018, and to Bagram Air Field in Afghanistan for Thanksgiving in 2019.
Fox News correspondent Jacqui Heinrich, the current president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, pointed out on X that the pool’s phones were not taken when Trump left Beijing after his state visit in May.
The move was later explained as a cybersecurity measure, as the phones used by journalists in China were placed in a metal-lined Faraday bag to prevent them from emitting any signals while the aircraft was aloft.
Most of the devices that were collected were so-called burner phones used only for the travel to China, as journalists had previously stored their regular devices in similar bags aboard Air Force One for use during the Philippines leg of the trip and while en route to Washington.
Separately, a flight restriction that had been imposed over Alaska around the time Air Force One had been scheduled to refuel there was lifted Thursday, raising questions as to the plane’s destination.
The most obvious candidate for a detour was North Korea. Trump spent the days before the summit musing that Kim Jong Un might join him when he met with China ’s Xi and Russia ’s Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in Manila that the president was “prepared” to meet the North Korean leader.
“It may not happen, but he’s prepared to do it,” Rubio said.
However on a call with reporters before the trip, senior U.S. officials said there were “no plans at all for engagement with North Korea.”
Trump relished the pageantry and attention that were lavished on his first two meetings with Kim, though neither sit-down resulted in the denuclearization deals he had promised to reach with the brutal autocrat.
He also met Kim for a third time during a visit to the Korean Demilitarized Zone and briefly became the first American president to set foot in North Korea.
The intrigue surrounding the president’s departure from China followed Trump’s participation in the first-ever meeting between an American president and the autocrats who have led the other two major nuclear powers for a combined 41 years.
Trump gave Putin a warm reception when he met with him for a bilateral meeting immediately preceding the three-way sit-down.
The U.S. president pointed, smiled and called out “Who is that? He’s my friend!” as he walked into a room with his Russian counterpart. The scene was captured by TV cameras that had been permitted in, even as journalists were barred from attending to prevent the leaders from being asked any uncomfortable questions, though a Russian official attributed the move to space constraints.
Trump said of Putin: “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they’ll come out of this.”
The Kremlin said after the meeting that the pair had discussed the ongoing war in Ukraine , and that Putin left in an “excellent” mood.
The White House offered no official readout of the sit-down, which lasted approximately 40 minutes.
Following the trilateral meeting, the Russian, Chinese and American governments released a four-point “peace declaration” reaffirming that a nuclear war should never be fought and vowing to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks.
The three leaders also pledged to advance reforms of the United Nations, to increase supplies of refined petroleum products for all countries and to uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.
The International Criminal Court in The Hague has issued arrest warrants for Putin and five other Russian officials. The Trump administration has been working to delegitimize and defund the ICC out of fear that Trump and his associates could be subject to war crimes charges over America’s campaign of airstrikes against alleged drug smugglers or an airstrike against an Iranian school that left over 100 children dead.

articles.title_orig: AMD shares slide after short-seller warns China ties could invite US scrutiny
articles.title_zh: AMD shares slide after short-seller warns China ties could invite US scrutiny
articles.content_orig:
Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices were down about 7% Wednesday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

articles.title_orig: Men guilty of abusing woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband
articles.title_zh: Men guilty of abusing woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband
articles.content_orig:
Four men have been found guilty of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged and secretly advertised her for sex on the internet, in the first trial of its kind in the UK.
Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife, Joanne Young, over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire.
Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.
Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, beamed at police as she left court wiping her eyes.
On the steps outside the court, Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, said the abuse had "cost me my life as I knew it".
"The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.
"This has resulted in a devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children."
She continued: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to.
"That choice makes them complicit in what was done to me and today's verdicts recognise that."
She said the verdicts were significant "more broadly for women and girls who have been abused by men," sending the message "that you can be believed and understood".
She urged the government to look at the law of consent "as a priority" so that women were "properly protected in the future", adding her abuse case raised "serious questions".
Judge Mr Justice Saini had asked for calm as the verdicts were read out, with Joanne Young sitting in the public gallery surrounded by her family, her hands clasped over her mouth.
She gasped as the first guilty verdicts were read out against Connor Sanderson-Doyle, who dropped his head as he was convicted of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration.
The jury of eight men and four women also convicted Wilkins of one count of assault by penetration.
Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at an earlier court hearing in February.
The judge commended Joanne Young and said she had shown "amazing bravery through these proceedings".
One police officer could also be seen sobbing as they left the court.
As all defendants were led from the courtroom after being told by the judge to expect lengthy jail terms when they are sentenced on 21 and 22 December, Joanne Young's family could be seen hugging.
Philip Young - who served as a Conservative Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 - drugged and raped his wife over 13 years and invited the men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.
He pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife.
James Foster, specialist Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) prosecutor, said: "This is the first time in the UK that a jury have convicted or been asked to consider a case of organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse, which has been organised by the husband."
The crimes of the former Tory councillor emerged after the highly publicised case in France of Gisèle Pelicot, whose husband, Dominique Pelicot, drugged and raped her and invited 50 other men to abuse her. Gisèle Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial.
Her husband was jailed for 20 years in France in 2024 and all the defendants were found guilty of at least one charge.
Police and prosecutors building the case against Philip Young sought the expertise of the French investigators to assist them in bringing him to justice.
Detectives discovered that Philip Young, whose most recent address was in Enfield, north London, had taken 480 intimate images and videos of his wife on 200 occasions and posted images online on at least 500 occasions – with the vast majority of these taken at the family home in Swindon.
The trial of the four defendants heard the investigation into Philip Young had begun after police were alerted to the fact he had uploaded extreme pornographic images to the internet in 2023.
Wiltshire Police said it was still looking for another man wanted in connection with alleged sex offences against Joanne Young.
They described him as being of "a large build, hairy, with scarring on the back of his head, prominent lips, short or shaved hair, and a distinctive tattoo on the left side of his chest".
Wiltshire Police added the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.
A police spokesperson said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.
"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption.
"These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

articles.title_orig: Leaders of China, Russia, US praise trilateral summit as 'success'
articles.title_zh: Leaders of China, Russia, US praise trilateral summit as 'success'
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
articles.title_zh: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.
The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.
In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.
Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".
Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.
In the same post, the president announced  he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.
While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".
He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".
Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.
The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.
Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".
Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.
China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.
Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."
Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".
It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."
"We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".
Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.
He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".
Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".
He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.
As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.
Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.
In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.
There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.
The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.
"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.
"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."
The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.
"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."
Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.
It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".
Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.
Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.
The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.
US lawmakers responded with frustration to Trump's warmth towards America's geopolitical adversaries.
"I was encouraged by some of the commitments that came out of the President's meetings in Asia, particularly the recognition that nuclear war must never be fought," Republican Senator John Curtis said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
But Curtis also said he was concerned about Trump's approach to the foreign leaders, adding that "Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends".
"We should not treat them as though they share our values or interests," Curtis, who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, added.
"Doing so risks undermining our national security, weakening trust with our allies, and sending the wrong message about where America stands."
Jeanne Shaheen, a ranking Democratic member on the same committee, chose harsher words in her comment.
"President Trump's 'friend' is a murderous war criminal," she wrote on X.
With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloons
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloons
articles.content_orig:
The still-unraveling scandal of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's extramarital affairs and the tech giant's potential role in its advanced semiconductor chips ending up in China present a legal minefield for Huang and Nvidia.
Federal and state prosecutors and Nvidia employees may target Huang and the company in court, where some shareholders have already taken action.
That's on top of a rapidly growing pile of probes by Republicans who control Congress now and Democrats who will have majorities in both the House and Senate come January.
"It's not going to get any better for Jensen Huang; it's going to get far worse," said Salvatore Graziano, a New York securities litigation attorney at Bernstein, Litowitz, Berger & Grossmann. His firm is looking at shareholder lawsuit opportunities against Nvidia and Huang.
[Huang] "faces the Department of Justice, the Securities and Exchange Commission and private litigation," Graziano said. "The criminal exposure is very serious. The SEC could bar him from being an officer. And the potential liability [from shareholder] lawsuits can be very large."
Huang's and Nvidia's legal exposure stems from three issues that led up to his shock resignation Nov. 12.
There's his alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who worked for Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company under investigation for diverting advanced Nvidia semiconductor chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules. That, in turn, has raised questions about whether Huang and Nvidia were aware of any diversions.
There are Huang's two other alleged affairs with Nvidia employees.
And there is the sharp drop in the company's stock price in the wake of the scandal. Nvidia's share price has fallen 19% since Nov. 8, when Huang sent a company-wide apology acknowledging extramarital affairs.
Huang last week retained the law firm Paul, Weiss and its attorneys Melinda Haag and Walter Brown to represent him. Haag is a former U.S. attorney in San Francisco, and Brown is also a former federal prosecutor.
Huang's spokesman at Trident, a crisis communications firm, declined to comment when asked if Haag and Brown are representing him in any potential criminal case and other questions about his legal exposure.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Last week, Nvidia retained the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation into Huang allegedly being targeted by a spy, as U.S. intelligence reportedly has concluded.
The civil liability Huang and Nvidia could face is underscored by a hearing Graziano, the securities attorney, attended Tuesday in U.S. District Court in San Francisco. A judge at the hearing approved a $175 million settlement from Seagate Technology Holdings to resolve a shareholder lawsuit alleging it concealed sales of hard-disk drives to Huawei in China in violation of export bans.
The Seagate settlement came three years after the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security — which is investigating Megaspeed's business with Nvidia — imposed a $300 million penalty on Seagate for its sales to Huawei.
Graziano said his law firm is "actively looking at securities law liability for Nvidia, Jensen Huang and other senior executives in the company given all the recent developments regarding their [potential] knowledge and facilitation of illegal chip sales to Chinese entities."
There is already a pending class-action shareholder lawsuit in San Francisco federal court against Nvidia and Huang by the Rosen Law Firm , for allegedly misleading and false statements related to Megaspeed and Alice Huang.
"Several hundreds of investors have contacted us and expressed an interest to join the case — investors of all walks of life, from mom and pops to investors with very large losses," Rosen attorney Phil Kim told CNBC in an email.
Katie Sweeten, a former federal prosecutor in the DOJ's National Security Division, said the question of "who knew what and when, and what was [Huang's] role" is potentially the biggest risk for Nvidia and him.
"Now DOJ can leverage their criminal authorities," Sweeten, a partner at Scale LLP, told CNBC's Kelly Evans on "The Exchange."
"They can bring grand jury subpoenas, search warrants for emails, bank accounts, personal devices, computers, things like that," Sweeten said.
While it is "not illegal to, you know, sleep with a spy ... it is illegal to pass certain types of information to a counterintelligence officer," she said .
Sweeten also pointed to potential export control violations, which "could be very serious."
She noted the DOJ can indict a company as well as its officials if there is evidence of criminality. Export control violations carry a maximum possible criminal sentence of 20 years in prison and "really large fines," she said.
"You can't send the company to prison, but they can face fines, civil penalties, debarment — where you can't export items down the line," she said.
One example of that came in July 2025, when the DOJ obtained a guilty plea and an agreement to pay more than $140 million from Cadence Design Systems for violating the Export Control Reform Act by unlawfully exporting semiconductor design tools to China's National University of Defense Technology, a school led by China's Central Military Commission.
Another potential legal risk for Huang comes from his planned appearances before Congress.
Huang is scheduled to give a closed-door interview Dec. 1 to three House committees. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., wants Huang's testimony before that panel to be public, and told CNBC Tuesday he hopes to have that happen "before Christmas."
Sweeten said Huang "has to be very careful" about what he says there because of the risk of being criminally charged with lying to Congress, and of saying something "that absolutely can become part of a criminal or civil investigation."
"I expect Huang to take the Fifth on most questions" from Congress, Jonathan Kanter, a former assistant attorney general in the DOJ's Antitrust Division, told CNBC, meaning Huang will likely use his constitutional right against giving testimony that could be used against him in a criminal case.
"With a Justice Department criminal investigation into Megaspeed already underway and more investigations possible, anything he tells Congress could be used against him," Kanter said. "His lawyers are likely to advise him against taking that risk."
Ben Heineman Jr., a former senior vice president and general counsel of General Electric , and a senior fellow at Harvard University, told CNBC that Nvidia's board will be scrutinized over its actions before it pushed Huang to resign.
Heineman cited the board's apparent lack of succession planning and what looks like weak oversight of Huang, including relating to personal conduct such as the two alleged affairs with Nvidia employees and with an executive of an Nvidia customer.
"When there is a sort of reasonable suspicion, they need to investigate it, and they don't appear to have done that," Heineman said.
Nvidia and Huang could face investigation from state attorneys general, including in California, where the company is headquartered.
On Tuesday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta told Bloomberg Television that the situation at Nvidia with Huang is "something that we're interested in." Bonta's office later told CNBC, "We are monitoring the situation."
Huang's alleged affairs with Nvidia employees also open the possibility of workplace litigation.
Ari Wilkenfeld, a Washington-area employment lawyer, said a consensual relationship between a chief executive and a subordinate "is not in and of itself illegal."
"The liability never comes from the existence of the relationship alone. It comes from whether it was genuinely welcome, what job benefits flowed from it, and what it did to everyone else in the building," Wilkenfeld said. articles.title_orig: Putin says Russia won't negotiate limited ceasefire with Ukraine after bridge strike
articles.title_zh: Putin says Russia won't negotiate limited ceasefire with Ukraine after bridge strike
articles.content_orig:
President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia will not negotiate with Ukraine on a limited ceasefire, citing a Ukrainian strike this week on a major bridge connecting Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin made the remarks to reporters in Russian after meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. He said he had discussed the possibility of a ceasefire in certain areas of Ukraine, but would not move forward with negotiations after Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, according to the Russian state news agencies.
The 12-mile bridge, which Putin ceremonially opened himself in 2018, is hugely symbolic as it links the Russian mainland with Crimea — territory that Russian forces occupied about four years earlier. The missile strike this week wasn't the first time Ukraine had targeted the piece of infrastructure, but it inflicted severe damage. Russia also struck two major bridges in Kyiv the same day.
Putin played down the bridge's strategic importance on Thursday and said he had heard the calls "from all sides" for a naval ceasefire or a suspension of strikes on energy facilities, but he ruled out direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing the attack on the bridge.
"Honestly, I discussed the issue with my colleagues at the Security Council, and I asked them to think about it and go back to the issue, so that we could reach some agreements," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency TASS. "However, we will not make agreements after strikes on the Crimean Bridge. We will respond to these strikes."
Putin vowed that Russia's retaliation for the strike on the bridge would be severe, TASS reported.
While Putin claims frequently to want peace, he denies that Russia started the war with his order for a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and Russia's attacks on Ukraine have been relentless.
It's not clear how much Ukraine came up in Mr. Trump's one-on-one meeting with Putin on Wednesday, or in the meeting with both Putin and Xi on Thursday. Last week, the White House said Ukraine wouldn't be a topic of discussion, but before he left for Asia, Mr. Trump said the three leaders would be discussing the war. The White House readout of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was sparse on detail, and did not mention Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff have been in Germany to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other European leaders about Ukraine and other topics.
Kushner said they discussed the "latest efforts to achieve a just, lasting and durable peace in Ukraine."
"We are grateful for his leadership, constructive engagement, and close partnership as we work together toward our shared goal of ending this terrible war and building a secure and prosperous future for Ukraine and Europe," Kushner posted to X .
Merz, speaking to reporters after the meeting, called the China summit a photo-op and said the trilateral format "will not bring peace" in Ukraine.
As he went to shake Putin's hand before an earlier meeting Wednesday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, Mr. Trump referred to the Russian leader as "my friend."
"Who is he?" the president said, pointing at Putin and smiling. "He's my friend."

articles.title_orig: Dow dives 800 points as Anthropic IPO milestone causes investors to take profits: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow dives 800 points as Anthropic IPO milestone causes investors to take profits: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks tumbled, falling to their lows of the session the very moment the widely anticipated artificial intelligence IPO Anthropic began trading .
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 1.3% after gaining as much as 2% earlier in the session. The S&P 500 shed 1.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 817 points, or 1.6%.
Anthropic , trading at the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, opened shortly before noon at $111.50 per share, a 34% pop. The stock was trading more than 10% off the first trading price and was last up 16%.
The major averages fell to session lows immediately following the start of trading for the much-hyped IPO, as investors appeared to take profits at the culmination of this moment for the AI trade.
The artificial intelligence company priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, above the expected range. That had chip stocks and other AI plays jumping in morning trading.
Chipmakers Nvidia and Broadcom gave up their gains, along with tech giants Microsoft and Meta Platforms . Advanced Micro Devices lost more than 8% after Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a short position in the name, pointing to alleged U.S. export control breaches that involve China.
"This was always going to be a critical test for the tech sector. Anthropic could be the new poster child for AI trade, especially after Nvidia headlines," said Aleks Spencer, Bogart Wealth CIO. "There's a lot here too that needs to be processed and digested, which translates to this period of uncertainty and volatility."
The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) , or Wall Street's so-called fear gauge, reached a day high of close to 29 — its highest level since March — shortly after Anthropic began trading and investors moved out of tech stocks. The index was last above 27.
"The enthusiasm comes in, and it's a great moment to sell the rally and take some profits," Spencer added.
The market has become more cautious on AI as of late, with investors focusing on whether heavy spending on the buildout will translate into meaningful profits. The iShares AI Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) has fallen 10% this month, and embattled AI bellwether Nvidia has dropped 27% while the company grapples with the resignation of its CEO Jensen Huang. Shares of CoreWeave, which had seen its bond yields trade above 16% earlier this month, is down 16% in November.
To be sure, some on Wall Street aren't too alarmed about the rollercoaster ride sparked by Anthropic's debut.
"Today doesn't matter," said Baird tech strategist Ted Mortonson, who deemed the day's action in Anthropic akin to that of a casino. "It's a blink of an eye of their journey. It's an important event, but how they navigate the next three years that will determine valuation."
While the major indexes took a leg lower immediately after Anthropic began trading at the Nasdaq, Interactive Brokers' chief strategist Steve Sosnick noted that the premarket rally faded before the artificial intelligence giant began trading.
"What we saw before that was the latest round of 'sell the rally' trading that has overtaken the more customary 'buy the dip' in recent days," he said.
Sosnick said that the rationale for the drop wasn't clear, though once the S&P 500 was able to break through a key support level in recent days, 7,300, that's when selling accelerated.
"The dam seemed to break once the big event was behind us," he added.
The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) topped 27 on Thursday, signaling uncertainty in the U.S. market.
It was last hovering at 27.94.
The stock market has been volatile as of late as investors have priced in macreconomic and geopolitical uncertainty. On Thursday, Anthropic listed its shares on the Nasdaq, sparking a selloff that rattled many areas of the market.
The S&P 500 fell further below its 200-day moving average on Thursday as stocks sold off following Anthropic 's initial public offering.
The broad-market index was last hovering around 7,273.98. That puts it about 74 points, or roughly 1%, below its 200-day moving average of 7,348.54.
"That's a big technical signal," Thomas Martin, a partner and senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments, told CNBC. "It has been above its 200-day moving average for a long time. And, if you're a trend follower, you say, 'okay, well, maybe if it breaks through, you have room to the downside.'"
The S&P 500's latest decline comes one day after its closed below its 200-day moving average for the first time since April 7.
Stocks rolled over to session lows nearly immediately after Anthropic began trading at the Nasdaq. While the AI giant opened 34% higher, it quickly eased from those levels — as enthusiasm around the company's public market debut withered.
The Dow tumbled to trade more than 1,000 points lower, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite were down more than 1% each.
The declines put the Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all down more than 3% for the month. Per Bespoke, this would be the first November since 2008 that all major indexes are down that much through Nov. 18.
Shares in frontier artificial intelligence laboratory Anthropic opened at $111.50, up 34.3% from its $83 initial public offering price, after raising a record $81 billion in the largest ever sale of stock by a company entering the public market for the first time.
At the opening price, Anthropic, led by CEO Dario Amodei, has a fully diluted market capitalization of roughly $2 trillion. San Francisco-based Anthropic trades on the Nasdaq Stock Market under ticker symbol ANT.
Amodei co-founded Anthropic less than six years ago, in 2021, alongside a handful of other researchers after the group collectively defected from OpenAI.
— Scott Schnipper, Ashley Capoot and Leslie Picker
Anthropic's debut on Thursday will serve as a key measure of just how much investors remain bullish on the artificial intelligence trade.
"It'll be an important barometer for investors' AI appetite," said Callie Cox, director of investment strategy at Plancorp. "AI stocks desperately need some wind at their backs, too ... Wall Street needs a sign that investors still believe in the potential for AI beyond already-elevated expectations."
"The challenge in that thesis is that hot IPOs rarely perform well right out of the gate, especially these days, when every company seems to be vying for a limited pool of capital to fund their AI strategy," she said. "While I wouldn't be surprised to see the stock market take cues from Anthropic's performance, I'd caution investors about trying to read the tea leaves from one event too much."
Enthusiasm around the Anthropic IPO is lifting the broader tech trade, especially those stocks that are direct proxies for the AI company. Here are the latest moves:
JPMorgan downgraded Alphabet corporate bonds to neutral from overweight, noting that "tighter valuations leave less room for outperformance relative to Amazon."
"Our base case assumes strong growth and eventual improvement in cash conversion, but [free cash flow] remains negative through 2028, requiring further financing while substantial liquidity and earnings keep leverage low," wrote credit analyst Erica Spear. "Alphabet's quarter exposed a widening divergence between accelerating Cloud demand and slowing Search growth, with weaker monetization of AI queries adding to uncertainty around the core earnings engine."
The three major averages began Thursday's session in positive territory.
The Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.5% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the S&P 500 gained 1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 230 points, or 0.4%.
U.S. gold futures for December delivery hit a low of $3,694.5 on Thursday, before recovering slightly to back above $3,700.
The low represented a level that the metal hasn't traded at since September 2025.
Gold is currently down 4.4% on the week, and tracking for its second straight weekly loss and the fifth negative one in six. The VanEck Gold Miners ETF (GDX) was down 1% in premarket trading Thursday.
— Gina Francolla and Davis Giangiulio

articles.title_orig: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.title_zh: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.content_orig:
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.
In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.
An image, meanwhile, showed six armoured vehicles, including tanks and bulldozers, around Salah al-Din road.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Multiple verified videos of the aftermath of the incursion on Thursday showed destruction, earth banks, and heavy vehicle tracks more than 1.2km beyond the Yellow Line.
That is believed to be the furthest Israeli troops have advanced into central Gaza since they occupied the so-called Netzarim Corridor before the ceasefire.
Some residents returned to check their properties following the Israeli withdrawal.
"The entire area has been destroyed, and we honestly do not know what to do," Abd Aliwa told Reuters news agency as he sat beside a pile of rubble.
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".
Gaza health officials said another two people were killed on Thursday by Israeli fire in eastern Gaza City, according to Reuters. There was no immediate comment from the IDF.
At least 1,662 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,710 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

articles.title_orig: There is no going back ‘to the way it was before’ the Iran war’s energy shock, IEA says
articles.title_zh: There is no going back ‘to the way it was before’ the Iran war’s energy shock, IEA says
articles.content_orig:
The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ⁠ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.
Energy markets have been rattled this year by the conflict, which has curbed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz , a route that ⁠typically carries about a fifth of global oil and ​liquefied natural ⁠gas supplies and is a key artery for Gulf exports.
“In my view, the energy world will never be the same again as it was before the Iran ⁠war,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said in an interview alongside the release of the agency’s World ​Energy ⁠Outlook 2026.
The conflict has resulted in cumulative ‌losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas supplies from the Gulf, the Paris-based agency said.
The annual outlook includes a range of scenarios based on existing and ‌proposed energy policies. This year it also examines how governments ‌and markets could respond to prolonged disruption in Hormuz.
Under a new Additional Response Case (ARC), the IEA said energy security concerns could speed up electrification, energy-efficiency measures and efforts to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels.
In that case, global oil demand in 2035 ⁠is 4.4 million barrels per day lower than under the agency’s Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), which reflects governments’ current policy intentions. Electric vehicles alone would displace more than 11 million bpd of oil demand.
Global oil demand falls to 97 million bpd in 2035 and 85 million bpd by 2050 under ARC, compared with just over 101 million bpd in 2035 under STEPS
Gas demand under ARC is more than 300 bcm lower than under STEPS.
The report said electrification is now cost-competitive across large parts of transport, ‌heating and industry, although inadequate grids, charging networks and power supplies could slow its rollout.
“Many ​countries are seeing electrification as a policy option for energy security. Instead of importing energy, ‌they decided to build energy at home,” Birol ⁠said.
Electricity’s share of final energy consumption is projected to approach 30% globally under STEPS, ⁠up from about 23% today, as transport, heating and parts of industry switch away from fossil fuels.
Alongside data centers, rising demand ‌for cooling is emerging as one ​of the strongest drivers of electricity consumption. For the ‌first time, demand for cooling in buildings has ​exceeded demand for heating, the IEA said, as higher temperatures and rising incomes drive rapid growth in air-conditioner use.
